background.definition: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is defined as a reduction of systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. An alternative to standing is the demonstration of a similar drop in blood pressure within 3 minutes using a tilt table in the head-up position at an angle of at least 60 degrees.

list.listitem: Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is a common condition. A systematic review of 13 studies that largely did continuous measurement of blood pressure found a prevalence of 28% in the general population (n=4157 participants) and 35% in a geriatric population. (n=1136 participants).
Predictors of OH include the number of prescribed medications, especially antihypertensives, and the presence of many comorbidities.
OH is also associated with a significantly increased risk of all-cause death, incident coronary heart disease, heart failure, and stroke.
See Differential Diagnosis table below.

Upon standing there is a shift of 500 to 1000 mL of blood from the thoracic organs to abdominal and pelvic organs, buttocks, and legs, causing the intrathoracic blood volume to fall by 26% to 30%. This causes an increase in the transmural capillary pressure in the lower body, an increase in fluid filtration into tissue spaces, and a decrease in plasma volume of up to 10%.

The result is a decrease in venous return to the heart, causing a fall in cardiac output of 15% to 30%, but the heart rate and total peripheral vascular resistanced increase by 25% to 45%. The result is an essentially unchanaged systolic blood pressure (SBP) and a slightly increased diastolic blood pressure (DBP) of 10% to 15%. This decrease in venous return to the heart activates two groups of pressure receptors, the high-pressure receptors of the carotid sinus and aortic arch and the low-pressure receptors of the heart and lungs. This in turn causes an increase in sympathetic outflow (causing constriction of resistance vessels and splanchnic capacitance vessels), and stimulation of the veno arteriolar axon reflex (constricting flow to the skin, muscle, and adipose tissue).

Also, during standing, contractions of leg and abdominal muscles compress both resistance and capacitance vessels, resulting in further elevation of peripheral vascular resistance. In addition, contraction of leg muscles, along with the venous valves, cause intermittent venous flow toward the right atrium. Continued upright posture also activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and vasopressin release.
OH occurs when any one of these physiologic compensatory mechanisms are compromised.
Acute alcohol ingestion may blunt the sympathetic nerve response in muscle normally activated in postural change.

The symptoms of OH are lightheadedness or dizziness beginning a few seconds after standing; blurred or tunnel vision; dull pain in the back of the neck and shoulders; weakness, cognitive impairment (thinking, concentrating), nausea, palpitations, tremulousness, vertigo, pallor, anxiety, and clammy feeling, all relieved by seating or lying down. C

Take a history for drugs or alcohol that might be causing hypotension, as well as for symptoms of diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure, chronic liver disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, adrenal insufficiency, cancer, or hypovolemia. C
Initial laboratory tests should include those for anemia, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, plasma cell dyscrasias, and vitamin B12 deficiency. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Antidepressant drugs: Selective serotonin receptor reuptake inhibitors, trazodone, monamin oxidase inhibitors, tricyclic antidepressants
Sympathetic blockers: like methyl dopa, clonidine, guanabenz
Vasodilators: like calcium channel blockers, hydralazine, nitroglycerine
Antiparkinson drugs: like levodopa, pramipexole, ropinirole
Acute, subacute or chronic autonomic failure
Hereditary: familial dysautonomia, dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency, aromatic
Metabolic: diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure, chronic liver disease, alcohol induced, vitamin B12 deficiency, adrenal insufficiency
Autonomic stressors: post-prandial dilation of splanchnic vessels, hot environment or bath, post vigorous exercise dilation of skeletal muscle vessels
intravascular hypovolemia: vomiting, diarrhea, hemorrhage, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes insipidus, salt-losing nephropathy, straining with defecation, urination, or heavy lifting
Vasodilator excess: mastocytosis, bradykinin excess, carcinoid syndrome

list.listitem: OH is defined as a reduction in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing.
An alternative to standing is the demonstration of a similar drop in blood pressure within 3 minutes using a tilt table in the head-up position at an angle of at least 60 degrees.
Autonomic function tests are helpful for the diagnosis of neurogenic OH by assessing the autonomic reflex arcs.

The symptoms of OH are the result of cerebral hypoperfusion and include lightheadedness or dizziness beginning a few seconds after standing, blurred or tunnel vision, dull pain in the back of the neck and shoulders ("coat hanger headache"), weakness, cognitive impairment (thinking, concentrating), nausea, palpitations, tremulousness, vertigo, pallor, anxiety, presyncope, syncope, and clammy feeling, all relieved by seating or lying down. But these symptoms can also occur with meals (post prandial hypotension), exertion, and prolonged standing, and can be worse early in the morning.

Take a blood pressure and heart rate after the patient has been supine for at least 5 minutes, and then ideally at both 1 and 3 minutes of standing. This will diagnose both immediate drops (which cause falls) and delayed onset BP drops. In a busy office practice, this may be too time consuming, and a single measurement seated and standing is a less sensitive alternative. Diagnosis of OH my require multiple measure ments on different days.
Finding orthostatic hypotension one minute after standing may be a more accurate predictor of dizziness and future adverse events.

Identify any prescription, over-the-counter, or illegal drugs or alcohol that may be causing the OH. See Differential Diagnosis table above. Ask patients when symptoms first appear, and whether the main problem is syncope, lightheadedness, or fatigue. Also ask at what time of day the symptoms tend to occur, what factors make the symptoms better or worse, and whether there are other organ systems that seem to be associated with the OH.

Ask about volume losses (dehydration, excessive vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding), to deterrmine possible acute contributors to OH. ****Hypovolemic patients may have symptoms like dry mucous membranes, dry and furrowed tongue, or weakness. Blood loss is suggested by history, of course, as well as supine hypotension, postural SBP decrease, or postural pulse increase ≥30 or severe dizziness.
Deconditioning (even short-term bedrest) and mild infections (like ruinary tract infections) in patients with impaired autonomic reflexes can dramatically worsen OH.
Search for history of congestive heart failure, malignancy, diabetes, and alcoholism.

An important clue of neurogenic OH are symptoms associated with autonomic stressors (meal, hot bath, exercise). A history of neurogenic causes should be sought, including diabetes mellitus, Parkinson's disease, and vitamin B12 deficiency.

Symptoms in men that suggest neurogenic OH include symptoms of urinarly retention (inability to pass urine with lower abdominal and /or suprapubic discomfort), severe constipation, decreased sweating, and erectile dysfunction. But these are nonspecific and common in the elderly. But the presence of significant OH without erectile dysfunction makes the diagnosis of neurogenic OH unlikely.

Neurologic examination that suggests neurogenic OH: decreased mental status (neurodegenerative disorders), cranial nerve evaluation (impaired downward gaze in progressive supranuclear palsy), pupil examination (Horner's or Adie's pupils), motor examination (Parkinson's motor rigidity, increased motor tone, and slow shuffling gait), sensory examination (polyneuropathies), ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, and signs of diseases that cause peripheral neuropathy (amyloidosis and malignancy).

Autonomic function tests are helpful in the diagnosis of neurogenic OH. They assess the autonomic reflex arcs. In autonomic dysfunction, the Valsalva maneuver causes an exaggerated and sustained decrease in BP without a compensatory increase in heart rate during the strain and lack of BP overshoot during the release. This response is diagnostic if neurogenic OH. But this requires continuous BP monitoring, which is not widely available. But few conditions besides neurogenic OH can explain profound OH without an adequate compensatory heart rate increase.

In nonneurogenic OH the blood pressure drop is usually associated with a compensatory increase in heart rate (>15/minute). History of nonneurologic causes should be sought, including cardiac pump failure, decreased intravascular volume (like symptoms with standing on awakening), chronic renal failure, chronic liver failure, cancer, adrenal insufficiency.

Symptoms of autonomic failure should be sought: including impotence, altered sweating (hypohidrosis or hyperhidrosis), dry eyes, dry mouth, dry nose, gastroparesis (bloating, nausea, vomiting of old food), bladder dysfunction (frequency, incontinence, hesitancy), constipation and/or diarrhea.
Order an ECG for patients with OH, and an echocardiogram if heart failure or structural heart disease is suspected based on the physical examination.
Initial laboratory tests include those for anemia, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, plasma cell dyscrasias, vitamin B12 deficiency, renal function, liver function.

When the history or physical examination suggest neuropathy (distal sensory loss, areflexia), an electromyogram and nerve conduction studies may be helpful, but normal nerve conduction studies does not rule out small-fiber neuropathy, which is associated with autonomic dysfunction. Syphylis serology and serum protein electrophoresis may be helpful in determinig the diagnosis.

Obtain an ECG and CBC for most patients; consider further evaluation for adrenal insufficiency, diabetes, Parkinson's, or other conditions as clinically indicated.

All of these recommended lifestyle, behavioral, and medication treatments for OH are based on very limited data. There is very little evidence based on long-term, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical tyrials.

Orthostatic hypotension in the elderly is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality.

The primary goals of treatment are to decrease the symptoms of OH, keep the patient ambulatory and functional, and decrease the risks of falls and syncope. This is accomplished by expanding plasma volume and increasing peripheral vascular resistance. Drug therapy must accompany aggressive lifestyle changes. Current drug treatment of OH is based on very limited data and few long-term randomized, controlled, double blind trials.

Drug therapy for OH can be complex. The medications for the treatment of OH can exacerbate hypertension and heart failure. If you do not feel comfortable adding the OH medications as you adjust the antihypertensive and heart failure medications, a referral to a hypertension specialist or cardiologist may be warranted.

The cornerstone of drug treatment is fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid), although data from randomized controlled trials is lacking. A Cochrane review identified 3 crossover trials with a total of 28 patients that showed some improvements in blood pressure reduction but without long-term follow-up and at uncertain risk of bias.

The startng dose is 0.1 mg/d. Doses >0.3 mg/d should be avoided because of corticosteroid-like effects. It transiently increases renal sodium and water retention and long-term increases sensitivity of arterioles to norepinephrine and angiotensisn II.

It is contraindicated in patients with heart failure or high risk for heart failure. Side effects include hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, fluid retention, and headaches. Potassium supplementation is often necessary. Supine hypertension at night is frequently seen, and may require decreasing the dose. Supine BP >180/110 should be avoided.

Midodrine is an alpha-1 agonist that causes venous and arterial constriction. Initial dose is 2.5 mg two to three times daily, increasing as tolerated to a final dose of 10 mg three times daily. It is usually given 30 to 60 minutes after meals (use caution with 20 mg dose). It can be helpful in postprandial OH. It should be avoided in patients with coronary artery disease and heart failure. Side effects include pruritus, uncomfortable piloerection (goose bumps), supine hypertension, and urinary retention in men. The first dose should be taken before getting out of bed in the morning, and the last dose before 6 PM, to avoid supine hypertension.
A randomized trial failed to show benefit of immediate midodrine therapy over placebo in patients undergoing early immobilization after hip arthroplasty.

Octreotide (somatostatin analog) inhibits the release of gastrointestinal peptides that have vasodilator and hypotensive effects. It causes vasoconstriction of splanchnic vessels and increases blood pressure in patients with autonomic failure. It is an option for patients with severe postprandial hypotension. It must be given SC or IV.
Prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors (like ibuprofen) taken with meals can be helpful in postprandial OH.
Anemia should be corrected. The increased intravascular volume that accompanies the increased hemoglobin can cause supine hypertension.

Drugs that are used less frequently are yohimbine (selective alpha-2 antagonist), desmopressin (vasopressin analog), clonidine (central acting alpha-2 agonist), metoclopramide (peripheral dopaminergic antagonist), fluoxetine (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor), and beta blockers.

An association has been reported between vitamin D deficiency and an increased likelihood of orthostatic hypotention (OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.14 - 1.63). However, a randomized trial of 688 patients comparing low dose vitamin D (200 IU/day) with high dose vitamin D (1000 to 4000 IU/day) found no difference in the number of orthostatic hypotension events.

In severe refractory OH from autonomic failure, ambulatory norepinephrine infusion via a port-a-cath and a programmable infusion pump has mobilized patients who were previously bedridden or wheelchair bound.
Intensive tratment of hypertension can cause hypotension, but an individual patient meta-analysis found that the reduction in CV and all-cause mortality was similar for patients with and without OH.
Increased salt and fluid intake is often recommended. For example, European Society for Cardiology guidelines recommend 2-3 liters of fluids and 10 grams of sodium chloride per day.

A systematic review identified 14 studied, of which 3 were randomized trials and only one of which had a duration of more than a week (2 months). Overall they found modest increases in blood pressure (12 mm Hg) and decreases in heart rate (4 beats per minute) with sodium supplementation.

A systematic review identified studies of non-pharmacological interventions for orthostatic hypotension. They concluded that resistance exercise, electrical stimulation, and lower limb compression bandaging were not effective. They found possible evidence supporting leg crossing, leg muscle pumping/contractions, bending forward, abdominal compression, and sleeping with the head up.
Refer to a cardiologist if arrhythmia or structural heart disease is suspected.

If the pateint has hypertension and OH and you feel uncomfortable adjusting the BP medications to avoid the large orthostatic BP drops and profound supine hypertension, referral to a hypertension specialist or cardiologist may be warranted.

An increased risk of falls is an important complication of OH. A study measured standing blood pressures following supine position 6 times in about 6 minutes after standing. While orthostatic hypotension was more common in the first 3 minutes (32% vs 16%), orthostasis at later time points was a stronger predictor of falling.
24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring may be useful to monitor the affects of the therapy.
